meta.title: Who really said "Our deepest fears are like dragons guarding our deepest treasure"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not Rilke. The line first appears in Sogyal Rinpoche's 1992 book The Tibetan Book of Living and Dying, as a paraphrase of a Rilke letter about dragons.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Our deepest fears are like dragons guarding our deepest treasure'?
meta.ogDescription: Not Rilke. It is Sogyal Rinpoche's 1992 paraphrase, from The Tibetan Book of Living and Dying — Rilke's dragons turn into princesses, not treasure guards.

answer.label: Not Rilke — a 1992 paraphrase by Sogyal Rinpoche
answer.authorDates: 1947–2019 · Tibetan Buddhist teacher, author of The Tibetan Book of Living and Dying
answer.sourceLine: The sentence in this form first appears in Sogyal Rinpoche’s The Tibetan Book of Living and Dying (Harper San Francisco, 1992), page 39, where it is introduced as something Rilke “has said” — a paraphrase, not a quotation. Its endnote points to Rilke’s Letters to a Young Poet, where the sentence does not appear.

source.excerpt: The Western poet Rainer Maria Rilke has said that our deepest fears are like dragons guarding our deepest treasure.
trail: Every popular copy runs sourceless. Goodreads ↗ attributes the line to Rilke with no work, edition or page, and carries its standing notice that community-submitted quotes are not verified.

The trail ends at a 1992 bestseller. The quote-research site Zitatforschung ↗ found the first attribution of this sentence to Rilke in Sogyal Rinpoche’s The Tibetan Book of Living and Dying, page 39, where it is introduced as something Rilke “has said”.

The book’s own endnote points somewhere else. It sends readers to Letters to a Young Poet ↗ (Vintage, 1986), page 92 — the passage where Rilke likens the dragons of our lives to princesses waiting to see us act with beauty and courage. No treasure, nothing guarded.

It escaped into pop culture still wearing Rilke’s name. In Ted Lasso season 2, episode 5, ‘Rainbow’, Rebecca reads the line off a dating app and credits it to Rilke — as a fan transcript of the episode ↗ records.
source.excerptNote: Note the framing: “has said that”, with no quotation marks. Rinpoche is summarising Rilke, not quoting him. Every later version drops the attributing clause and adds the quotation marks — which is precisely how a paraphrase becomes a quotation.
source.rightsHolder: Sogyal Rinpoche’s estate and HarperCollins Publishers
source.rightsNote: The wording people quote originates in a book first published in 1992, so it is under copyright in the United States. Rilke’s own Briefe an einen jungen Dichter (Insel-Verlag, Leipzig, 1929) is public domain in the US as a pre-1931 publication — but that text does not contain this sentence, and the twentieth-century English translations of it are themselves separately in copyright.

author.name: Sogyal Rinpoche
author.heading: The writer whose sentence this actually is
author.metaLine: 1947–2019 · Tibetan Buddhist teacher · founder of the Rigpa network
author.bio: Sogyal Rinpoche was born in Trehor, Kham, in eastern Tibet in 1947 and founded Rigpa, an international network of Buddhist centres. His The Tibetan Book of Living and Dying, assembled with editors Patrick Gaffney and Andrew Harvey and published in 1992, became a global bestseller — more than three million copies in dozens of languages — and carried this sentence to a very large readership under Rilke’s name. He stepped back from Rigpa in 2017 after former senior students alleged abuse, and died in Bangkok in 2019.

copyAttribution: "Our deepest fears are like dragons guarding our deepest treasure." — not Rainer Maria Rilke. The sentence first appears in Sogyal Rinpoche, The Tibetan Book of Living and Dying (Harper San Francisco, 1992), p. 39, offered as a paraphrase of Rilke. Rilke's own letter of 12 August 1904 likens the dragons of our lives to princesses waiting to see us act with beauty and courage — no treasure, no guarding. Via Quotle.info

misattribution.heading: How Rilke got the credit
misattribution.intro: This is a clean, fully documented case of a paraphrase hardening into a quotation. The writer who coined the sentence said openly that he was reporting Rilke’s idea; everyone downstream dropped the reporting and kept the quotation marks.

items.why: No edition of Rilke has ever been shown to contain this sentence. Wikiquote’s sourced Rilke page ↗, which organises his lines by the work they come from, does not carry it in any section.

Rinpoche did give a citation — an endnote pointing to Letters to a Young Poet. But as Zitatforschung ↗ shows, the page it names carries the dragons-into-princesses passage instead; the treasure sentence is not there.
Goodreads ↗ runs it as Rilke with no work, edition or page, under its own notice that community-added quotes are not verified. AZQuotes and QuoteFancy print it the same way.
A 2014 HuffPost essay ↗ on Tibetan Buddhist teachings about impermanence states flatly that Rilke said it — in an article otherwise drawing on Rinpoche’s own book.

misattribution.truthLine: The sentence is Sogyal Rinpoche’s, written in 1992 to summarise Rilke — and Zitatforschung ↗ found no attribution to Rilke earlier than that book.

context.heading: What Rilke actually wrote
lead: Rilke did write about dragons — once, memorably, in a letter to the young officer cadet Franz Xaver Kappus dated 12 August 1904. He invokes the old myths in which a dragon turns into a princess at the last moment, and suggests that perhaps every dragon in our lives is a princess waiting to see us act, just once, with beauty and courage; perhaps everything terrible is, at bottom, something helpless asking for our help. The letters were published in 1929 by Insel Verlag in Leipzig, three years after Rilke’s death, as Briefe an einen jungen Dichter.

There is no treasure in that passage and nothing is guarding anything. The hoard-and-guardian image — fear as a dragon coiled on top of something you want — is a different idea, and a more transactional one: Rilke asks you to love the frightening thing, while the popular line promises a reward on the other side of it. That second, tidier thought is the one that travels.
context.detailsSummary: How the paraphrase escaped the book
detailsBody: Sogyal Rinpoche’s sentence carries an endnote, and the book keeps that citation in later editions. But readers quoting the line rarely carried the endnote with it. Within two years, according to Zitatforschung, the sentence was appearing in quotation marks as Rilke’s own words with no mention of the book it came from — among the instances it cites are Dawna Markova’s No Enemies Within (Conari Press, 1994) and Caitlin Matthews’ Singing the Soul Back Home (Element, 1995).

Music and television did the rest. Ray Wylie Hubbard, who has said repeatedly that Letters to a Young Poet changed his life, closed “The Messenger” on his 1994 album Loco Gringo’s Lament with the same fear-as-dragon-over-treasure image, credited to Rilke. And in 2021 the line turned up on a dating app in Ted Lasso, where Rebecca reads it out as Rilke and Keeley approves.

German-language versions were re-translated back out of Rinpoche’s English rather than from anything Rilke wrote, which is why the German circulating text (“Unsere größten Ängste sind die Drachen, die unsere tiefsten Schätze bewahren”) matches no line in Rilke’s collected letters.
context.pull: Rilke’s dragon becomes a princess. The internet’s dragon sits on a pile of gold.

sourcesVerified.claim: This sentence is a pseudo-Rilke quotation: it was first attributed to Rilke in English in 1992 in Sogyal Rinpoche's The Tibetan Book of Living and Dying, p. 39, worded 'The Western poet Rainer Maria Rilke has said that our deepest fears are like dragons guarding our deepest treasure'; the cited support was p. 92 of Stephen Mitchell's translation of Letters to a Young Poet, where the dragons-into-princesses passage appears instead; Rilke's German original is the letter of 12 August 1904 in Briefe an einen jungen Dichter (Insel, 1932 printing), p. 48; within two years the line was circulating in quotation marks as Rilke's own, e.g. Dawna Markova, No Enemies Within (Conari Press, 1994), p. 250 and Caitlin Matthews, Singing the Soul Back Home (Element, 1995), p. 20; post dated 16 September 2021.
Wikiquote's sourced page for Rainer Maria Rilke does not contain the sentence 'Our deepest fears are like dragons guarding our deepest treasure' in any section.

Goodreads displays 'Our deepest fears are like dragons guarding our deepest treasure.' attributed to Rainer Maria Rilke with no source work cited, alongside a notice that quotes are community-added and not verified.
Rilke's Letters to a Young Poet were written 1902-1908 to officer cadet Franz Xaver Kappus (1883-1966) and first published in 1929 by Insel Verlag, Leipzig, three years after Rilke's death.
The Tibetan Book of Living and Dying was published in 1992, became a bestseller, and has been printed in more than three million copies across dozens of languages.

Sogyal Rinpoche was born in 1947 in Trehor, Kham, Tibet, founded the Rigpa network of Buddhist centres, wrote The Tibetan Book of Living and Dying (1992), stepped back from Rigpa in 2017 after abuse allegations by senior students, and died on 28 August 2019 in Bangkok.
The Internet Archive holds the Harper San Francisco 1992 first edition of The Tibetan Book of Living and Dying by Sogyal Rinpoche, edited by Patrick Gaffney and Andrew Harvey (ISBN 0062507931).
The Internet Archive holds Rilke's Briefe an einen jungen Dichter, with Franz Xaver Kappus, published by Insel-Verlag, Leipzig, 1932.
The Internet Archive holds the Vintage Books (New York) 1986 edition of Rilke's Letters to a Young Poet, the edition whose page 92 Sogyal Rinpoche's endnote cites.
The Internet Archive holds Dawna Markova, No Enemies Within: A Creative Process for Discovering What's Right About What's Wrong, Conari Press, Berkeley, 1994.

A 2014 HuffPost article on Tibetan Buddhist teachings about death and impermanence states 'Rainer Maria Rilke said that our deepest fears are like dragons guarding our deepest treasure' as the author's own assertion, without noting Sogyal Rinpoche as the source of the phrasing.
In Ted Lasso season 2, episode 5, 'Rainbow', Rebecca says a man on the Bantr app 'has just quoted Rilke' and reads out 'Our deepest fears are like dragons guarding our deepest treasures'.
Ray Wylie Hubbard's song 'The Messenger', from his 1994 album Loco Gringo's Lament, invokes the fears-as-dragons-guarding-treasure image as a reference to Rilke.

Quote Investigator's Rainer Maria Rilke category page lists no article about this quote (dragons, fears or treasure); the only Rilke article listed concerns 'The Purpose of Life Is To Be Defeated by Greater and Greater Things'.
